title: What Makes People Actually Respond to Your Emails (Boomerang analysis, 5.3M messages; fetched via summarizer)
rule: Aim for 50-125 words; ask one to three questions (more than three reverses the gain); slightly positive or slightly negative tone beats neutral and beats effusive; moderate flattery helps, excessive hurts. 2016 data, Gmail productivity-tool users.
example: Boomerang's pizza test: the moderately warm email beat both the flat and the effusive one.
llm_tell: Uniformly effusive/agreeable affect and over-long replies sit on the losing side of both findings.

title: What's the Best Word Count & Length for Cold Emails (Hunter, 34M cold emails)
rule: For cold email, Hunter's data put 20-39 words highest in reply rate and calls the Boomerang range outdated and warm-email-heavy. Vendor data; the sweet spot depends on warm vs cold. Secondhand via search summary; Boomerang third-grade-reading-level and 75-100 word 51% figures are also secondhand and unverified.
llm_tell: Model emails default to 150-300 words regardless of relationship.

title: Help Scout: customer service phrases to avoid and what to say instead
rule: Replace stock phrases with the specific problem plus the action taken. Name what went wrong, own it, say what you did. Say what you can do, not 'unfortunately I can't'. 'Anything else?' only after the problem is actually solved. Don't redirect the customer to another channel.
example: Bad: 'Our apologies for any inconvenience this may cause.' Good: 'I'm sorry the export failed and deleted your report. I've restored it, and it should be in your account now.' Bad: 'I'm sorry you feel that way.' Good: 'You're right, that charge shouldn't have happened, and I'm sorry. I've refunded it today.'
llm_tell: 'We apologize for any inconvenience', 'Thank you for reaching out', 'I understand your frustration' with no named problem and no action.

title: Intercom: our best practice guide to customer support (truncated page)
rule: Personalize, sound human, be proactive. Stock answers are easy for customers to spot and make the team look bad; use macros only for questions that recur. When the fix isn't ready, send a quick personalized acknowledgment instead of silence. Page was truncated in the search summary; the full tone section was not read.
llm_tell: Macro-like replies with no reference to the customer's specifics.

title: OSU news: the 6 elements of an effective apology (Lewicki et al. 2016, 755 people, scenario experiments)
rule: Ranked by effect: 1 acknowledge responsibility, 2 offer repair, 3 (tied) express regret, explain what went wrong, declare you won't repeat it, 4 request forgiveness (cut it first). More elements rated better. Scenario ratings of written apologies, not field outcomes. Source is the university press release.
example: Study wording: 'I was wrong in what I did, and I accepted responsibility for my actions.' / 'I'll fix what is wrong.'
llm_tell: Model apologies lead with regret ('I'm so sorry for any confusion') and skip ownership and repair, which are the two strongest elements; they also add 'please forgive me'-style softeners.

source: https://www.mitsloanreview.mit.edu (Packard, Moore, McFerran 2018; read via search summary only)
title: 'I'll be there for you' / 'we' vs 'I' in customer service language (JMR 2018 / MIT SMR)
rule: Agents who write 'I' are read as acting on the customer's behalf and raised satisfaction and purchases; 'we' (common in scripts) was worse; 'you' made no difference or hurt. Based on 1,000+ real service emails from one Canadian retailer plus experiments. Secondhand summary; the HBR URL I tried returned 404.
example: 'I will look into this' rather than 'We will look into this'.
llm_tell: Corporate 'we' and 'our team' in replies that should be one named person doing one thing.

title: LiveChat: sorry for the inconvenience (vendor blog; figures traced to no original)
rule: Consistent theme across vendor blogs: a specific acknowledgment of what went wrong plus a concrete action beats a generic 'sorry for the inconvenience'. Cited figures (Boomerang Commerce two in five satisfied; Nottingham plain apology beat cash; SMARI 45% vs 23%) could not be traced to originals; do not quote them.
llm_tell: 'Sorry for the inconvenience' as a stand-alone apology.

title: Coursera: AI cover letter red flags recruiters spot fast (page held no list)
rule: Null result: the page claims recruiters spot AI letters 'in seconds' but the text I could fetch lists no phrases and quotes no recruiter. Not usable as evidence.

title: GradConnection: how to identify AI-generated graduate resumes and cover letters
rule: Recruiters flag repeated phrases and sentence structures, transitional paragraph openers, and claims with no numbers, projects or company references. Fix: one specific example from the applicant's own experience, the applicant's own tone, facts checked. Seen only through a search summary.
example: Stock openers named in search results: 'I am excited to apply', 'I am writing to express my interest'; paragraph starters 'Furthermore', 'Moreover'.
llm_tell: Stock opener, buzzwords ('expert', 'cutting-edge'), same sentence skeleton in every paragraph, no company-specific detail, no figures.

title: TopResume survey of 600 US hiring managers (also Resume Now 900 HR pros; CV Genius 625 UK managers; all via search summary)
rule: Managers are anti-generic more than anti-AI: Resume Now reports 62% say uncustomized AI resumes often lead to rejection and 78% say personalized detail signals effort. Rejection-for-AI-use ranges from about 20% (TopResume) to majority distrust (CV Genius). Vendor surveys with different questions; figures not comparable and not verified against the reports.
llm_tell: A letter that could be sent to any employer unchanged.

title: The Register: Originality.ai LinkedIn study (8,795 posts of 100+ words)
rule: Originality.ai's own detector flagged 54% of long posts as likely AI, rising after ChatGPT; average post length rose 107%. The detector counts heavily AI-edited text. The article reports no engagement figures and names no style tells, so the '45% less engagement' claim in a blog is unverified. Annoying content types named: performative charity, personal success generalized into life advice.
llm_tell: Longer posts that turn a personal anecdote into a general lesson. Detector-based share is an estimate by a vendor that sells the detector.

title: LeadDev guide to Slack etiquette (with Backbase, Workable, The Muse; read via search summary)
rule: Put the question in the first message instead of a bare 'hello'; merge points into one message instead of a run of short ones; reply in threads; use @channel only when it matters to everyone in it. No measured data; style guidance.
example: Not 'Hi' then wait; 'Hi, is the staging deploy blocked on the migration?'
llm_tell: Multi-paragraph formatted Slack messages with headings and bullets, and a greeting plus sign-off, where a human sends one or two lines in plain text.
